speaker: Scott Kirby
title: Scott Kirby - United Airlines CEO
question: In commercial aviation, how do automated family seating systems handle late bookings when adjacent seats are scarce?
guest: We try to move to any open seats on the airplane to at least put kids together with at least one adult in the party. The places where we have challenges are when the kids are in different records, which you'd be surprised how often people have their kids booked in different records, so we don't know that they're the same, or sometimes just when the flights are completely full and there aren't enough seats. But we'll also try to do it in reverse age order. So we'll try to find the youngest first and put them with one of the parents. Sometimes we'll split the party if there's two parents—we'll try to find two seats here and three seats there. It's not 100% because sometimes there's just not seats on the airplane. But we now run automation to do that for customers in advance, so that as they book, it just shows up as these seats.

points.core: Automation runs before check-in to pair children with an adult using open seats.
points.note: Accept: advance automated seat assignment across open cabin inventory rather than waiting for gate agents. Do not credit: claiming airlines only fix family seating manually at the gate.

points.core: Systems prioritize seating the youngest children first in reverse age order.
points.note: Accept: placing infants or toddlers with a parent before older children. Do not credit: generic statements about seating families together without age prioritization.

points.core: Multi-parent families are split into smaller adjacent seat clusters when needed.
points.note: Accept: dividing a large family into separate groups like two seats here and three seats there so each child sits with one parent. Do not credit: assuming the entire family must sit in one single row.

points.core: Automation fails when children are booked on separate reservation records.
points.note: Accept: unlinked PNRs or separate booking confirmations preventing the system from recognizing family members. Do not credit: blaming only full flights or airline fees without mentioning separate records.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Automated family seating systems generally work on a best-effort basis, and late bookings are where they most often fall short.

When a reservation includes a child (typically 13 or under, flagged by date of birth), the airline's seating engine scans for adjacent open seats at booking and again at later trigger points, usually a few days before departure and at the check-in window. Airlines such as United and American run this dynamically, and some hold back blocks of seats, often in the rear rows, specifically for late-booking families.

When adjacent seats are scarce, the system typically escalates in steps. It first opens seats normally restricted or sold for a fee, such as preferred seats, though usually not extra-legroom or premium cabins. If that fails, it prioritises seating each child next to at least one adult rather than keeping the whole party together, splitting the family across rows or the aisle. If no solution exists, the case goes to gate agents, who manually reseat or ask volunteers to swap. Some carriers, such as United, offer a free rebooking onto another flight with adjacent seats.

Guarantees usually exclude basic-economy edge cases, aircraft swaps, and separate bookings.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Automated airline seating systems accommodate late-booking families through layered inventory controls and pre-departure optimization. First, dynamic seat maps proactively block select contiguous rows from solo travelers based on historical demand, revealing those held seats only when a reservation includes a young child. If standard pairs are exhausted, the booking engine automatically unlocks unsold, fee-based preferred or extra-legroom economy seats at no charge, prioritizing pairing each child with one accompanying adult rather than seating larger families in a single row.

When no adjacent economy seats exist at booking, the airline's departure control system places the reservation on an automated watch list. Between 72 and 24 hours before takeoff, seating algorithms claim pairs freed by cancellations or elite upgrades and consolidate scattered empty seats by relocating unassigned or non-paying solo passengers into equivalent window or aisle spots, while enforcing exit-row rules. If the cabin remains completely fragmented, the system flags the booking for gate agents or offers free rebooking onto another flight.

noweb.answer: When families book late on nearly full flights, automated airline seating systems first tap reserved blocks of contiguous seats—typically held back in the rear of the cabin—that remain hidden from general selection until departure nears. Rather than attempting to seat an entire group together, the algorithm prioritizes pairing each young child with at least one accompanying adult on the same reservation. If standard free seats are exhausted, modern dynamic systems automatically unlock preferred or extra-legroom seats within the same cabin at no additional charge. Simultaneously, background optimization engines reshuffle unassigned inventory, holding or reassigning travelers without confirmed seat selections—such as basic-economy passengers—to consolidate scattered single seats into side-by-side pairs while protecting paid seat assignments and elite members. When genuine cabin fragmentation prevents an automated match, the system flags the booking on a priority airport queue for gate-agent intervention, such as soliciting seat-swap volunteers, or automatically offers the family a fee-free transfer to another flight with open adjacent seating.

When adjacent seats are scarce on a late booking, automated family seating systems usually work through a series of fallbacks.

First, the algorithm checks whether a child (typically 13 or under) is on the same reservation as an adult. It then looks for any adjacent pair, often including extra-legroom or "preferred" seats that would normally cost extra. United's 2023 policy works this way: the seat map opens those seats to families at no charge.

If no adjacent pair exists, the system may hold the family for reassignment at check-in or close to departure. By then it can move solo travelers who didn't pay for a specific seat, release seats it had blocked, or reshuffle the cabin as no-shows and upgrades clear. Gate agents handle what's left by hand, often by asking other passengers to swap.

If adjacency still can't be guaranteed, some airlines, United among them, let the family move to another flight in the same cabin without paying a fare difference. The U.S. DOT's 2024 proposed rule would require fee-free adjacent seating, or a choice of a refund or free rebooking. As far as I know, that rule hasn't been finalized, so practices still differ by airline.

points.why: The system searches for an available child–adult seat pair at booking and may defer reassignment to check-in if that search fails.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: When adjacent standard seats are scarce on late bookings, automated family seating systems work through a tiered fallback process rather than simply splitting the party. First, dynamic seat-map engines unlock inventory normally hidden from general travelers—such as seats held back under airport or family blocks—and often open paid "preferred" seats in the same cabin at no extra charge so a young child can sit beside an adult. If no adjacent pair is open at purchase, the system typically queues the reservation for automated batch sweeps in the days leading up to departure, taking advantage of cancellations, elite upgrades, and re-optimizing unassigned solo passengers to create pairs. When a late-booked flight remains completely saturated, the software generally avoids displacing passengers who paid for specific seats; instead, carriers with family-seating guarantees offer fee-free rebooking onto another flight with adjacent seats, or escalate the reservation to airport gate agents, who control the final blocked rows and can arrange voluntary seat swaps before boarding.

noweb.answer: When adjacent seats are scarce for late bookings, automated family seating systems rely on a tiered set of strategies to keep children seated next to at least one accompanying adult. First, airlines typically hold back dedicated blocks of seats—often near the rear of the cabin—from general selection so the algorithm can assign them to late-booking families. If those are exhausted, many systems automatically unlock paid preferred or extra-legroom seats at no additional charge, or split larger families into smaller adult-child pairs rather than trying to seat the entire party together. During pre-departure optimization sweeps, the software may also reassign solo travelers who have not paid for specific seats or do not hold elite status to open up adjacent pairs. When a flight is so full that none of these automated adjustments succeed, the system flags the booking for airport check-in or gate agents, who resolve it manually before boarding by rearranging seat assignments or asking other passengers to swap.

When a family books late, automated seating systems look for available seats that put each young child next to at least one accompanying adult. If there’s no room for the whole family in one row, the system may seat them in smaller groups across several rows. Some airlines hold seats for families or rerun their seating process before departure so they can use seats freed by cancellations or other changes.

If the system still can’t find an adjacent pair, airline staff may step in at check-in or at the gate. The outcome depends on the airline’s policy, applicable rules, and which seats are available on the flight.
